blocks.quote: “I sent Dan a text almost as soon as I left the house. 'Love you. Take care.' He would see right through it; would know I was anxious. I just couldn't shake the feeling that something was seriously wrong. I wanted to turn and run back, step inside and triple-check. I needed this to be real.”
blocks.zh: Emma 离家几乎 immediately text Dan："Love you. Take care." 她知道 Dan 会 see right through it，知道她 anxious。她 just couldn't shake the feeling that something was seriously wrong。她想 turn and run back，step inside and triple-check。She needed this to be real。
blocks.why: Love you. Take care. = Emma's correction attempt—she's reaching for Dan, trying to prevent the loop. "He would see right through it; would know I was anxious" = Emma's self-awareness—Dan knows her. "I needed this to be real" = Emma's desperate need for the loop to be real (not a dream). This is Emma's first active correction: she's not just reliving, she's trying to change.
blocks.tip: Love you. Take care. = Emma's correction attempt; "see right through it" = Dan knows Emma; "I needed this to be real" = her desperation.

blocks.quote: “'For fuck . . .' The cyclist glared over his shoulder at me and I felt my whole body lurch. It just couldn't be. How?”
blocks.zh: "For fuck . . ." cyclist glared over his shoulder at her，她 felt her whole body lurch。"It just couldn't be. How?"
blocks.why: The cyclist near-miss repeats (from ch04/ch18)—same event, same cyclist. "It just couldn't be. How?" = Emma's disbelief—the loop is repeating despite her attempts to change. "my whole body lurch" = her physical recognition of the loop—her body remembers even if her mind hopes it's different. The cyclist is the loop's first checkpoint: if the cyclist appears, the loop is repeating.
blocks.tip: For fuck . . . = the loop's first checkpoint; "It just couldn't be. How?" = Emma's disbelief; the cyclist is the loop's confirmation.

blocks.quote: “I'm not sure I should have caffeine,” I said, almost to myself.
“Headache?” the barista asked sympathetically.
“Something like that,” I said, chewing my lip as I stared at the chalkboard behind him. “I'll have a freshly squeezed orange juice, please.”
blocks.zh: Emma says "I'm not sure I should have caffeine," almost to herself. Barista asks "Headache?" She says "Something like that" and orders "freshly squeezed orange juice."
blocks.why: Emma changes her order (orange juice instead of hazelnut latte)—her second correction attempt. "Something like that" = she's not lying (she does have a "headache" of sorts—the loop). The barista's "My mum has the bad migraines" + "I think I've got some [pain pills], I should not really give, but if you haven't?" = the barista's kindness (he's offering free pain pills). Emma declines ("Oh no, I'm all right, thanks though"). "On house" (free muffin) = the barista's generosity. This is Emma's first small change in the loop: different drink, same kindness from the barista.
blocks.tip: freshly squeezed orange juice = Emma's correction (different drink); "Something like that" = her truth (she has a "headache" of sorts); the barista's kindness = the loop's constant.

blocks.quote: “'Please yes,' I typed back, leaping at the opportunity to talk to her.”
blocks.zh: "Please yes," Emma typed back, leaping at the opportunity to talk to Hattie。
blocks.why: "Please yes" = Emma's correction—she accepts Hattie's lunch invitation (in ch04, she left Hattie's message unopened). "leaping at the opportunity" = Emma's urgency—she needs Hattie. This is Emma's third correction: she's actively seeking connection (Hattie) instead of avoiding it. The loop is giving Emma a chance to do things differently.
blocks.tip: Please yes = Emma's correction (accepting Hattie's lunch); "leaping at the opportunity" = her urgency; this is her third correction attempt.

blocks.quote: “Would today be exactly the same? And was it like the tree falling in the wood? If I wasn't there would it still happen?”
blocks.zh: "Would today be exactly the same? And was it like the tree falling in the wood? If I wasn't there would it still happen?"
blocks.why: This is the chapter's philosophical question—Emma is asking if the loop is deterministic. "Would today be exactly the same?" = her fear that nothing she does changes the outcome. "tree falling in the wood" = the classic philosophical question (if a tree falls in a forest and no one is there to hear it, does it make a sound?). Emma is asking: if she changes her behavior, does the loop change? Or is the loop fixed regardless? "If I wasn't there would it still happen?" = her fear that Dan will die regardless of what she does. This is the loop's central tension: determinism vs free will.
blocks.tip: tree falling in the wood = Emma's philosophical question about determinism; "If I wasn't there would it still happen?" = her fear that Dan will die regardless.

blocks.quote: “Emma @Dan Just checking in with you! Message me back OK!”
“Emma @Dan X X X”
blocks.zh: Emma @Dan "Just checking in with you! Message me back OK!" / "X X X"
blocks.why: Emma @Dan "Just checking in with you!" = Emma's correction—she's messaging Dan (in ch04, she didn't message him during the commute; in ch07, she messaged "Don't worry about the sausages! I'll shop!"). "Message me back OK!" = her urgency—she needs Dan to respond. "X X X" = kisses (British text convention)—Emma is expressing love via text. This is Emma's correction: she's reaching for Dan, trying to prevent the loop. But Dan doesn't respond (in the chat interlude, there's no reply from Dan). The loop continues.
blocks.tip: Just checking in with you = Emma's correction; "Message me back OK!" = her urgency; "X X X" = kisses; Dan doesn't respond—loop continues. Emma's corrections：text Dan "Love you. Take care." (ch04: no text), orange juice (ch04: hazelnut latte), "Please yes" (ch04: left Hattie's message unopened), brisker at meeting (ch06: "Under control?" panic). Emma is actively trying to change the loop. But the loop's events (cyclist, same messages, same Arthur meeting) still occur. The loop is partially deterministic. "tree falling in the wood"：Emma's philosophical question about determinism. If she changes her behavior, does the loop change? Or is the loop fixed regardless? "If I wasn't there would it still happen?" = her fear that Dan will die regardless. This is the loop's central tension. Emma @Dan "Just checking in with you!"：Emma's correction—she's messaging Dan (in ch04, she didn't; in ch07, she messaged "Don't worry about the sausages!"). "Message me back OK!" = her urgency. "X X X" = kisses. Dan doesn't respond (no reply in chat). The loop continues. barista's kindness：the barista gives Emma a free muffin ("On house") and offers pain pills. This is the loop's constant—kindness persists even as the loop repeats. Emma's "Your smile reminds me of my daughter" = her reaching for connection. "Would today be exactly the same?"：Emma's growing awareness that the loop is deterministic. She changes small things (drink, text) but the big events (cyclist, Arthur meeting, committee) still occur. The loop allows small variations but not big changes. This is the novel's determinism question. loop structure：ch17 (loop reset, "Again.") → ch18 (loop #2, Emma tests reality) → ch20 (loop #3, Emma tries to change). The loop is giving Emma more agency each iteration, but the outcome (Dan's death) remains fixed. The loop's central tension: can Emma change the outcome? Or is Dan's death inevitable?

blocks.quote: “Seeing Hayley in the lobby of the publisher did something to me. The urge to tell someone, a friend, overwhelmed me.”
blocks.zh: Seeing Hayley in the lobby did something to Emma；the urge to tell someone, a friend, overwhelmed her。
blocks.why: urge to tell someone = Emma's need to share her loop-awareness—she can't carry it alone. "a friend" = Hayley is her friend (from ch06: "Hayley, a friend who'd acquired one of my first authors"). "overwhelmed me" = the need is physical, not chosen. This is Emma's first attempt to break the loop's isolation: she wants to tell someone. But Hayley won't listen (later: "I don't have time to be a friend"). The loop isolates Emma.
blocks.tip: urge to tell someone = Emma's need to share; "a friend" = Hayley; overwhelmed = physical need; the loop isolates Emma.

blocks.quote: “'Ow,' I shrieked, grabbing my arm.”
“'Sorry,' I whispered, holding up my arm. 'Just . . . checking.'”
blocks.zh: "Ow," Emma shrieked, grabbing her arm. "Sorry," she whispered, holding up her arm. "Just . . . checking."
blocks.why: "Ow" = Emma jabbing her pen into her arm to check if this is real (pain = reality). "Just . . . checking" = her euphemistic explanation—she's checking if she's in a dream. The ellipsis (Just . . . checking) shows her hesitation—she can't explain what she's checking. This is Emma's loop-verification: pain = reality. Everyone swiveled toward me, Melissa's speech tailing away—Emma's outburst disrupts the meeting. "Sorry" = her apology for the disruption.
blocks.tip: Ow = Emma's pain check (reality verification); "Just . . . checking" = her euphemism; the ellipsis shows her hesitation; everyone swiveled = the meeting's disruption.

blocks.quote: “'Or you could come off Twitter altogether, Arthur?' I suggested, my voice bright.”
blocks.zh: "Or you could come off Twitter altogether, Arthur?" Emma suggested, her voice bright。
blocks.why: "come off Twitter altogether" = Emma's suggestion (different from ch06's bursary scheme lie)—she's trying to change the meeting's outcome. "voice bright" = Emma performing confidence (like ch06's "straightening my shoulders"). But this suggestion backfires: Arthur refuses, Linda is angry, Melissa threatens to pause the contract. Emma's correction attempt makes things worse—she's changing the loop's events but not the outcome (Arthur still storms out). This is the loop's irony: Emma can change small things (drink, text) but big changes backfire.
blocks.tip: come off Twitter altogether = Emma's suggestion (backfires); "voice bright" = her performance; the suggestion makes things worse—Arthur storms out, Linda is angry.

blocks.quote: “As Linda got into the lift with Arthur she held her hand up. 'I need to talk to my client alone,' she told me, and then added in a hiss, 'I will talk to you later today.'”
“'I will talk to you later today.'”
blocks.zh: Linda held her hand up: "I need to talk to my client alone." Then added in a hiss: "I will talk to you later today."
blocks.why: "I need to talk to my client alone" = Linda excluding Emma—she's asserting her authority over Arthur. "in a hiss" = Linda's anger—she's furious at Emma for disrupting the meeting. "I will talk to you later today" (repeated) = Linda's threat—Emma is in trouble. This is the loop's professional consequence: Emma's correction attempt (suggesting Arthur come off Twitter) has made Linda angry. The loop allows small changes but punishes big ones.
blocks.tip: I need to talk to my client alone = Linda excluding Emma; "in a hiss" = her anger; "I will talk to you later today" = her threat; Emma's correction backfires.

blocks.quote: “I don't have time to be a friend.”
blocks.zh: "I don't have time to be a friend," Hayley said。
blocks.why: Hayley's rejection is the chapter's emotional climax—Emma reached out for help, and Hayley refused. "I don't have time to be a friend" = Hayley's priority (fixing the meeting) over Emma's need (sharing the loop). "I've got to go back upstairs and help fix all this" = Hayley is professional, not personal. Emma's "I really need to talk to you" vs Hayley's "I don't have time to be a friend" = the gap between Emma's need and Hayley's availability. This is the loop's isolation: Emma can't tell anyone, and the people she reaches for can't help.
blocks.tip: I don't have time to be a friend = Hayley's rejection; Emma's need vs Hayley's availability; the loop isolates Emma—she can't tell anyone.

blocks.quote: “'No,' I said carefully. 'No, not dying. It can wait . . .'”
blocks.zh: "No," Emma said carefully. "No, not dying. It can wait . . ."
blocks.why: not dying = Emma's literal answer (she's not dying—Dan is, but Emma doesn't know how to explain). "It can wait" = Emma's deferral—she'll tell Hayley later (but she won't, because the loop will reset). "carefully" = Emma's caution—she's choosing her words. This is the loop's tragedy: Emma has information (the loop, Dan's death) but can't share it. "It can wait" = the loop's cruel irony—Emma thinks she has time, but the loop will reset and she'll forget.
blocks.tip: not dying = Emma's literal answer; "It can wait" = her deferral; the loop's cruel irony—Emma thinks she has time, but the loop will reset. Emma's correction backfires：Emma tries to change the meeting's outcome (suggesting Arthur come off Twitter instead of the bursary lie). But this makes things worse—Arthur storms out, Linda is furious, Melissa threatens to pause the contract. The loop allows small changes (drink, text) but punishes big ones. This is the loop's determinism: Emma can change small things, but the big events (Arthur's storm-out, Linda's anger) are fixed. "Ow" (pen jab)：Emma jabs her pen into her arm to check if this is real. "Just . . . checking." = her euphemism. This is the loop's physical verification: pain = reality. Emma is checking if she's in a dream. The pain confirms she's real (or in a very real loop). Hayley's rejection："I don't have time to be a friend" = the loop's isolation. Emma can't tell anyone about the loop, and the people she reaches for can't help. Hayley is professional, not personal. Emma's "I really need to talk to you" vs Hayley's "I don't have time to be a friend" = the gap between Emma's need and Hayley's availability. "It can wait"：Emma's deferral—she thinks she has time to tell Hayley later. But the loop will reset and she'll forget. This is the loop's cruel irony: Emma thinks she has time, but she doesn't. The loop will reset, and she'll lose this information. "No, not dying"：Emma's literal answer. She's not dying—Dan is (but she doesn't know how to explain). This is the loop's central asymmetry: Emma knows, Dan doesn't. Emma can't share what she knows. loop structure：ch20 (loop #3, Emma tries to change small things) → ch21 (loop #3 continues, Emma's big change backfires). The loop is giving Emma more agency each iteration, but big changes backfire. The loop's central tension: can Emma change the outcome? Or is Dan's death inevitable? The loop suggests: small changes are allowed, big changes are punished. Emma's tragedy: she can't make the one change that matters (preventing Dan's death) without making things worse.

blocks.quote: “'I'm not,' I protested, a fraction too loudly. The waiter in the reindeer ears looked over. 'OK,' I admitted, gulping wine, I was almost down to the final mouthful. 'I need to talk to you.'”
blocks.zh: Emma 否认 being crazy intense，但声音有点 too loudly；waiter in reindeer ears looked over；她 admitted，gulping wine，almost down to the final mouthful："I need to talk to you."
blocks.why: crazy intense = Emma's state—she's desperate to share the loop. "a fraction too loudly" = she can't modulate her voice—her urgency leaks out. "gulping wine, almost down to the final mouthful" = Emma drinking fast (her anxiety). "I need to talk to you" = her core need—to share the loop with someone who loves her. This is Emma's first attempt to break the loop's isolation.
blocks.tip: crazy intense = Emma's state; "gulping wine" = her anxiety; "I need to talk to you" = her core need.

blocks.quote: “'It's Monday again. Today. Everything is happening all over again.'”
blocks.zh: "It's Monday again. Today. Everything is happening all over again."
blocks.why: It's Monday again = Emma's attempt to explain the loop—she's reliving Monday. "Everything is happening all over again" = her description of the loop. Hattie's response ("Yeah. That's how the weeks work. It's Monday every Monday.") shows she doesn't understand—she's literalizing Emma's claim. "No, you don't understand" = Emma's frustration—Hattie can't grasp the loop's reality.
blocks.tip: It's Monday again = Emma's loop explanation; Hattie's literal response shows her inability to understand; "No, you don't understand" = Emma's frustration.

blocks.quote: “'Maybe that's what your dream was about?' Hattie mused. 'Giving you a second chance?'”
blocks.zh: "Maybe that's what your dream was about?" Hattie mused. "Giving you a second chance?"
blocks.why: Hattie's interpretation: the loop is a dream giving Emma a second chance. "mused" = Hattie's thoughtful tone—she's humoring Emma but also offering a rational explanation. "Giving you a second chance?" = Hattie's reframing—the loop as opportunity, not curse. This is Hattie's character: she's logical, kind, and tries to find the positive. But Emma knows it's not a dream ("It wasn't a dream"). Hattie's interpretation is comforting but wrong.
blocks.tip: Maybe that's what your dream was about? = Hattie's interpretation (loop as dream/gift); "Giving you a second chance?" = her reframing; Emma knows it's not a dream.

blocks.quote: “Dan told me he's barely seen you.”
“She didn't meet my eye.”
blocks.zh: Hattie told Emma that Dan said he's barely seen her. She didn't meet my eye。
blocks.why: Dan told me he's barely seen you = Dan has been talking to Hattie about Emma's absence (behind Emma's back, or at least not directly to Emma). "She didn't meet my eye" = Hattie's discomfort—she's delivering Dan's message, which is painful. This is the marriage's communication breakdown: Dan talks to Hattie about Emma, not to Emma. "Have you wondered whether maybe it's just stress?" = Hattie's concern—she's worried about Emma. "This thing... Maybe it's a bit of a sign you need to ease up a little, take some time for yourself?" = Hattie's advice (ease up, take time). Emma's "It's not a thing" = her denial.
blocks.tip: Dan told me he's barely seen you = Dan's indirect communication; "She didn't meet my eye" = Hattie's discomfort; "maybe it's just stress" = Hattie's concern; Emma's denial.

blocks.quote: “'Have we ever?' I replied.”
blocks.zh: "Have we ever?" Emma replied to the waiter's "Have you had enough time, ladies?"
blocks.why: "Have we ever?" = Emma's response to the waiter's "Have you had enough time, ladies?" The question is existential: have we (Emma and Hattie) ever had enough time? Have we ever had enough time for anything? This is the chapter's final question—Emma and Hattie, like Emma and Dan, are running out of time. The loop is consuming everything. "Have we ever?" is the novel's central question: has Emma ever had enough time? The answer is no—she's always rushing, always late, always missing things.
blocks.tip: Have we ever? = Emma's existential question; have we ever had enough time? The answer is no—Emma is always rushing. This is the loop's central question. Hattie as rational voice：Hattie is Emma's anchor—logical, kind, trying to find the positive. But she can't understand the loop. "Maybe that's what your dream was about? Giving you a second chance?" = her interpretation (loop as dream/gift). Emma knows it's not a dream. Hattie's rationality is both comforting and insufficient. "Dan told me he's barely seen you"：Dan has been talking to Hattie about Emma's absence—behind Emma's back, or at least not directly to Emma. This is the marriage's communication breakdown: Dan talks to Hattie, not to Emma. Hattie is the intermediary. "Have we ever?"：Emma's existential question—have we ever had enough time? The answer is no. Emma is always rushing, always late, always missing things. The loop is consuming everything. This is the novel's central question. "No one knows what goes on behind closed doors"：Hattie's own marital concern (Ed finds medical stuff hard). This is Hattie's hidden struggle—she and Ed are going through something (medical). Emma notices but doesn't pursue (her pattern: notes but doesn't act). chat interlude：Jas/AuthorLou's messages show Emma's work world intruding. "Jas @Emma What happened? Linda is M-A-D." = Arthur crisis escalating. "AuthorLou @Emma" (4 messages) = AuthorLou's needy demands. Emma is the hub of a wheel that's coming off. loop structure：ch20 (loop #3, Emma tries to change) → ch21 (loop #3 continues, Emma's big change backfires) → ch22 (loop #3 continues, Emma tries to share the loop with Hattie). The loop is giving Emma more agency and more isolation simultaneously. She can change small things, but she can't share the loop. The loop isolates her.

blocks.quote: “Writing this sends me spinning back to this time last year and the night that changed everything.”
blocks.zh: "Writing this sends me spinning back to this time last year and the night that changed everything."
blocks.why: spinning back = Dan's memory is physical—writing the letter pulls him back to the balcony fall. "the night that changed everything" = the fall as catalyst. This is Dan's recovery narrative: the letter begins with the fall, not the anniversary. The anniversary is the frame; the fall is the content. Dan is writing from a place of transformation—he's looking back at his lowest point.
blocks.tip: spinning back = Dan's physical memory; "the night that changed everything" = the fall as catalyst; this is Dan's recovery narrative.

blocks.quote: “I’d been out on the balcony, back against the handrail, telling some story to some stranger I didn’t care about. Arms wide, I’d been gesturing extravagantly when the bottle fell from my grip and in a jerky movement to try to catch it, I’d overbalanced and lost control completely.”
blocks.zh: Dan was on the balcony, back against handrail, telling some story to some stranger he didn't care about. Arms wide, gesturing extravagantly, the bottle fell from his grip and in a jerky movement to try to catch it, he overbalanced and lost control completely。
blocks.why: back against the handrail = Dan's physical position—leaning back against the railing, vulnerable. "telling some story to some stranger I didn't care about" = Dan's disconnection—he's performing for strangers, not connecting. "gesturing extravagantly" = his body language—arms wide, uncontrolled. "the bottle fell from my grip" = the drink (alcohol) is the catalyst. "in a jerky movement to try to catch it, I'd overbalanced" = Dan's attempt to catch the bottle caused the fall. "lost control completely" = the fall as loss of control—both physical (tumbling over) and metaphorical (his life). Whether this is a suicide attempt or accident is ambiguous: "lost control completely" could be either. The ambiguity is the point—Dan's fall is both accidental and intentional.
blocks.tip: back against the handrail = Dan's vulnerability; gesturing extravagantly = his uncontrolled body language; overbalanced and lost control completely = the fall as both accident and metaphor; the ambiguity (suicide attempt vs accident) is deliberate.

blocks.quote: “I told Hattie I couldn’t recall any of it, but that isn’t true. I remember falling backward, I remember the thoughts I had as I fell through the air.”
blocks.zh: Dan told Hattie he couldn't recall any of it, but that isn't true. He remembers falling backward, the thoughts he had as he fell through the air。
blocks.why: I told Hattie I couldn't recall any of it, but that isn't true = Dan's lie to Hattie—he remembers but pretends not to. "I remember falling backward" = Dan's suppressed memory—he remembers the fall. "the thoughts I had as I fell through the air" = Dan's interior during the fall—what was he thinking? The implication: he was thinking about dying. This is the novel's darkest moment—Dan's fall is likely a suicide attempt (or at least, he was not trying to prevent it). "I remember the thoughts I had as I fell" = Dan's awareness during the fall—this is not an accident's amnesia, this is a deliberate act's memory. The ambiguity is the point: Dan may have wanted to fall.
blocks.tip: I told Hattie I couldn't recall = Dan's lie (he remembers); "I remember falling backward" = his suppressed memory; "the thoughts I had as I fell" = the implication of suicidal intent. This is the novel's darkest moment.

blocks.quote: “That fall transformed everything for me. Life looked different after that night. I’d wanted to change but that night gave me the strength to do it.”
blocks.zh: "That fall transformed everything for me. Life looked different after that night. I'd wanted to change but that night gave me the strength to do it."
blocks.why: transformed everything = the fall as catalyst—Dan's near-death experience changed his perspective. "Life looked different after that night" = Dan's perception shift—surviving the fall made life look different. "I'd wanted to change but that night gave me the strength to do it" = Dan's recovery narrative—the fall gave him the push he needed. This is Dan's turning point: from depression to recovery. The fall is both his lowest point and his catalyst.
blocks.tip: transformed everything = the fall as catalyst; "gave me the strength to do it" = Dan's recovery narrative; the fall is both lowest point and catalyst.

blocks.quote: “I lived for those days with the two of you in between my other life, the sad single-dad bachelor I knew I never wanted to be.”
blocks.zh: "I lived for those days with the two of you in between my other life, the sad single-dad bachelor I knew I never wanted to be."
blocks.why: lived for those days = Dan's purpose—Emma and Poppy are his reason to live. "in between my other life" = Dan has two lives: the one with Emma/Poppy (purposeful) and the single-dad bachelor life (lonely). "the sad single-dad bachelor I knew I never wanted to be" = Dan's self-awareness—he doesn't want to be a single dad, he wants to be with Emma. This is Dan's recovery: he's working to be worthy of Emma and Poppy.
blocks.tip: lived for those days = Dan's purpose; "sad single-dad bachelor" = his unwanted identity; "I knew I never wanted to be" = his self-awareness.

blocks.quote: “You are my very favourite human.”
blocks.zh: "You are my very favourite human."
blocks.why: very favourite human = Dan's closing—Emma is his favorite human (not just "love" but "favorite human"). "very" intensifies; "favourite" = British spelling; "human" = Dan's choice of word—he's not saying "woman" or "wife" but "human," which is more fundamental. This is Dan's purest statement of love—after the fall, the therapy, the reconciliation, "you are my very favourite human" is his final valuation. The letter ends here.
blocks.tip: very favourite human = Dan's purest statement of love; "human" (not "woman/wife") = more fundamental; this is the letter's closing. the balcony fall：Dan's fall from the balcony is the novel's darkest moment. "I remember falling backward, I remember the thoughts I had as I fell through the air" = Dan remembers (he lied to Hattie about not recalling). The implication: this was a suicide attempt (or at least, Dan was not trying to prevent it). "I'd wanted to change but that night gave me the strength to do it" = the fall as catalyst. This is Dan's turning point. "I told Hattie I couldn't recall any of it, but that isn't true"：Dan's lie to Hattie—he remembers but pretends not to. This is Dan's pattern: he hides his pain ("leaving the room" in ch12). But he's honest in the letter—he tells Emma the truth. "That fall transformed everything for me"：the fall as catalyst—Dan's near-death experience changed his perspective. "Life looked different after that night" = his perception shift. reconciliation："The second first kiss in Wimbledon Park" = Dan and Emma's reconciliation. "You let me stay" = Emma's trust. "I love being home" = Dan's gratitude. "You are my very favourite human"：Dan's purest statement of love. After the fall, the therapy, the reconciliation, this is his final valuation of Emma. "human" (not "woman/wife") = more fundamental. loop structure：This letter is from 2012 (9 years before the present-day loop). Dan's recovery narrative shows the marriage's arc: crisis (ch12) → separation (ch16, ch19) → fall (ch23) → recovery (ch23). The present-day loop (ch02–ch22) is the loop's "After"—Dan dies, Emma relives. The past letters show what was lost: a marriage that recovered, a man who overcame depression, a family that came back together. The loop's tragedy: all of this recovery is erased when Dan dies on Dec 3, 2021. Emma relives the day Dan died, but she can't relive the years of recovery. The loop only gives her Dec 3.
